title: Should Aston Villa Hijack Tottenham’s Transfer Plans For This €40m Rated Striker?
description: Aston Villa could face competition from Tottenham Hotspur for Benfica striker Vangelis Pavlidis, who reportedly wants to fulfil his ambition of playing in the Premier League. According to Portuguese n...
fullText:
Aston Villa could face competition from Tottenham Hotspur for Benfica striker Vangelis Pavlidis, who reportedly wants to fulfil his ambition of playing in the Premier League. According to Portuguese newspaper A Bola, via Sport Witness, the Greek international remains interested in English football and would welcome an opportunity to leave Lisbon if Benfica approve his departure.

Pavlidis hasn't forced an exit, though. The 27-year-old continues to perform professionally for Benfica, but his preference for a Premier League move could become relevant if an interested club submits an acceptable offer.

Benfica previously placed a €40 million valuation on the forward despite his €100 million release clause. Several major European clubs explored opportunities during the previous transfer window, including Barcelona, AC Milan, Juventus and Beşiktaş. However, those approaches failed to produce an agreement.

Marco Silva considered Pavlidis an important part of his plans and made retaining the striker a priority. Consequently, Benfica refused to sanction his departure despite interest from several established European sides.

His performances explain that resistance. Pavlidis registered 30 goals during his previous campaign and has already recorded 14 goals and three assists this season. Those numbers give interested clubs a clear indication of his finishing ability and attacking contribution.

Tottenham's interest could develop into something more concrete. A Spurs scout reportedly watched him during Benfica's meeting with FC Porto, suggesting that the London club continues to assess his performances.

LISBON, PORTUGAL – JULY 30: Vangelis Pavlidis of SL Benfica in action during the UEFA Europa League Qualifier match between SL Benfica and St. Gallen at Estadio da Luz on July 30, 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal. (Photo by Gualter Fatia/Getty Images)

Aston Villa have several attacking options, including Nicolas Jackson, Tammy Abraham and young Brian Madjo. That competition could discourage Unai Emery from pursuing another centre-forward, particularly if his existing players remain available.

However, squad numbers don't always tell the complete story. Jackson's fitness, Abraham's performances and Madjo's development will influence Emery's recruitment decisions. Pavlidis offers considerably more established goalscoring experience than a teenage prospect, although signing another senior striker could restrict opportunities elsewhere.

Tottenham could have a clearer opening if Richarlison leaves after falling outside Roberto De Zerbi's plans. Pavlidis would then compete with Dominic Solanke and Omar Marmoush for attacking responsibilities.

My opinion? Aston Villa shouldn't dismiss this opportunity, but they must establish their actual requirements before entering negotiations. Jackson deserves an opportunity to establish himself, while Abraham and Madjo need clarity about their positions.

Spending €40 million on Pavlidis makes little sense unless Emery identifies a genuine need for another starting striker. Tottenham currently appear better positioned to explore the transfer, while Villa should monitor developments without committing significant resources prematurely.

title: 'Best midfielder in the world': Liverpool star told he's as good as Zidane
description: Liverpool have not had an overly easy time of it, results-wise, at the start of the 2026/27 season. Andoni Iraola has presided over only two victories in his opening five Premier League games - agains...
fullText:
Liverpool have not had an overly easy time of it, results-wise, at the start of the 2026/27 season.

Andoni Iraola has presided over only two victories in his opening five Premier League games - against newly promoted Ipswich Town as well as former club Bournemouth.

It is going to take a while for the Basque tactico's ideas to come across but there's no doubt we've seen promising signs already.

Alexander Isak for example is back among the goals on a more regular basis while improvements have been made to the backline too.

Liverpool are possessed of world-class talent in the midfield meanwhile - and it's only a matter of time before the Anfield side start firing on all cylinders.

The club offered new contracts to both Ryan Gravenberch and Dominik Szoboszlai over the past few months.

Szoboszlai, 25, has hit the ground running for club AND country this season - hitting an unbelievable goal in the EFL Cup victory over Tottenham.

The Hungarian captain has carried on that fine form during the international window - excelling in the weekend win against Giorgi Mamardashvili's Georgia where Milos Kerkez scored the only goal of the game.

Szoboszlai's performance was so good in the heart of midfield that Georgian coach Giorgi Tsetsadze - in charge of top-flight side Rustavi - told Hungarian media that the Liverpool man reminded him of a certain Zinedine Zidane on the night.

"Looking at Dominik Szoboszlai, I thought of Zinédine Zidane – and not because of his hair…" he tells Nemzeti Sport.

"Seriously, his performance was almost perfect both in attack and defense.

"He was constantly looking for opportunities to pass forward, he was rushing towards the goal, trying to score, and what is especially important, he not only played forward in the middle of the field, but also gave dangerous passes in the final third.

"I think he is one of the best midfielders in the world at the moment."

Zidane is one of a select band of players to win the UEFA Champions League, the FIFA World Cup as well as the Ballon d'Or and goes down as one of the all-time greats of the game.

Iraola will be hoping to tap into those Zizou-like traits on a more regular basis once Szoboszlai returns from international duty.

title: Man City whistleblower to lose witness protection
description: Portuguese computer hacker who released documents which led to the Premier League investigation into Manchester City set to lose his witness protection despite fears for his life.
fullText:
The Portuguese computer hacker who released documents which led to the Premier League investigation into Manchester City is set to lose his witness protection despite his fears he could be assassinated.

Football Leaks founder Rui Pinto released a tranche of confidential football documents, including emails and financial records relating to the English Premier League side.

In 2018, he shared documents with German magazine Der Spiegel, which used them for investigations into City's finances and alleged breaches of financial fair play rules.

Last week, City were found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, which they have appealed.

Pinto became part of Portugal's witness protection programme in 2020 after agreeing to co-operate with authorities and provide files obtained through the Football Leaks operation.

He posted on X on Friday, external that the decision to terminate his participation in the programme on 10 October has put him in a "life-threatening situation".

The 37-year-old said it had left him with no alternative but to relocate to an undisclosed location for an indefinite period because of "multiple death threats" and "the serious risk of an assassination attempt".

BBC Sport has approached the Commission for the Protection of Victims of Crimes in Portugal for comment.

Pinto has described himself as a whistleblower, but was convicted in Portugal of offences including illegal access to data and attempted extortion and given a four-year suspended sentence.

He wore a bulletproof vest during his first trial in 2020, which was also subject to heightened security measures.

Earlier this year, he was acquitted in a second trial of 241 counts of illegally accessing email accounts belonging to a number of sports bodies in Portugal, including Benfica.

On Wednesday, Pinto turned his attention to Fifa president Gianni Infantino, saying he had "become a cancer on football" and should "have no place in the future of the game".

Pinto repeated allegations from 2018 that Infantino intervened to help City and Paris St-Germain avoid financial fair play sanctions from European football's governing body Uefa.

Infantino's position has recently come under increased pressure following controversial plans to sell stakes in the governing body's competitions, such as the World Cup, to private investors.

A statement from Pinto's lawyers released on Friday said the decision to end his participation in the witness protection programme left him at heightened risk, noting legal proceedings stemming from the leaks remained ongoing, including the case against Manchester City.

Pinto has set up a fundraising page to help him "survive this serious situation", which he claims was "created by the Portuguese State".

title: Timely recognition or long overdue? How Gross is proving all-time bargain
description: Named the Premier League's player of the month for September, BBC Sport looks at Brighton star Pascal Gross' impact both this season and over the past nine years during his two spells at the club.
fullText:
Having been named the top-flight's player of the month for September, it leads to the question of whether Brighton midfielder Pascal Gross may be one of the best value-for-money signings in Premier League history.

In fact the 35-year-old has effectively cost the Seagulls minus £3m - and been involved in 85 Premier League goals over two spells.

Nobody has been involved in more top-flight goals than Gross this season - six in five games.

He was Brighton's first Premier League signing in 2017 for a reported £3m from Ingolstadt and left for his boyhood club Borussia Dortmund in 2024 for £8m.

But in a surprise move he returned to Albion in January for about £1.7m.

Since Gross first joined Brighton nine years ago, only three players have created more chances in the division than his 562 - Bruno Fernandes, Kevin de Bruyne and Mohamed Salah.

And that includes the 18 months he was away from the Premier League.

So has Gross been underrated all this time?

Former England midfielder, and BBC pundit, Danny Murphy doesn't think so.

"The Premier League is shown worldwide, and he has been a part of that for so many years during a time when Brighton have been a shining light," he said.

"You don't have to play for a big-six team to be appreciated in the Premier League. Gross is not under the radar, because people know how good he is."

Gross was Albion's first signing after they sealed promotion to the top flight.

A little-heralded German from relegated Ingolstadt, nobody could have anticipated the impact he, nor Albion, would go on to have.

For one he has played in 73% of their top-flight games since 1983.

"There's an argument Gross is pound-for-pound the best value player in the Premier League over the last 10 years, especially when you look at his goal involvements," said BBC Radio Sussex commentor Johnny Cantor.

"However, he also drives standards in training, sets a high bar and is a huge influence in the dressing room.

"Technically he is excellent, has superb delivery but also possesses an awareness, popping up in spaces all around the pitch. Managers have leaned on him, team-mates respect him, and fans of all generations adore him.

"He will surely be remembered as one of the best Albion players of the modern age."

As well as his notable record of creating chances, Gross has put in more successful crosses, including corners, than any other player in that time (483) despite Trent Alexander-Arnold and James Ward-Prowse attempting more.

For passes played into the box - including those crosses - he is fourth.

Gross also features seventh for assists with 51 to go with his 34 goals in 252 Premier League games.

All the more remarkable when you consider his journey with Brighton appeared over two years ago when he went home to join his beloved Borussia Dortmund.

Albion supporter Maz Mirzadeh said: "When he left for Dortmund, it was like going through a heartbreak and seeing an ex go back to their childhood sweetheart.

"He's outrageously good and massively underappreciated.

"If you watch him play, you would think someone's put him in slow-motion settings, but what he lacks in pace, he makes up in superior football IQ, technical brilliance and working harder than any other player on the pitch."

Gross played 66 times for Dortmund, scoring one goal and assisting 17 times, but on 2 January 2026, he came back to Brighton.

Aged 34 at the time, many wondered if it was more of a romantic career swansong.

"There may have been concerns that he may not have been able to recreate the impact of his first period at the Amex but that has been dispelled already," added Cantor.

Only Chelsea's Joao Pedro can match Gross' goal contributions this season in the top flight (both three goals, three assists).

Remarkably Gross has run 

The midfielder - who retired from international football after the World Cup - has also played every single minute for Brighton in all competitions, eight games so far.

Former Liverpool and Fulham midfielder Murphy said: "He's an intelligent footballer, with a great football IQ.

"You can see that he has grown into that version of himself over the years. That happens in football - it happened to me - when you know what you can't do, as much as you know what you can do.

"So, you don't see him trying to beat people on the outside with his pace. Instead he loves a little chop, or a Cruyff turn to give himself space and time, or to play a quick first-time pass around the corners. That's why he always seems to be in space.

"His versatility tells you about his intelligence as well. He is able to play as a full-back, central midfield or, recently, as more of a 10. He is scoring and making goals.

"I am sure this won't be his last season with Brighton but, even if it was, he is already going to be remembered as one of the Brighton greats by their supporters for what he has given so far to the club, especially with him coming back and doing what he is doing. It is nothing short of remarkable."

Gross has also created more Premier League chances (15) this season than anyone else to help Brighton to third in the table.

This form led to him being the sixth oldest player to be named Premier League player of the month.

Seagulls fan Mirzadeh added: "Even in his 'unc' era, he's showing the Premier League's elite how it's done.

"If he was called Pascal Silva and played for a top-six club he might get the recognition and respect he truly deserves."

title: Downing Street responds after Prime Minister 'backs' Manchester City owners amid charges
description: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been accused of 'backing' Manchester City's owners after the club was found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules, prompting a statement from Downing Street
fullText:
Downing Street has released a statement after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham was accused of 'backing' Manchester City's embattled owners. City were found guilty of 114 breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between 2009 and 2018, with an independent commission determining that they had inflated revenue and reduced costs by £900 million ($1.187 billion), issued 'sham' contracts, and misrepresented accounts throughout the nine-year period.

The club strongly deny the charges and maintain that there is a 'comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence' that proves their innocence. Should City fail in their appeal, speculation has mounted that their Abu Dhabi owners, including Sheikh Mansour, could be compelled to sell the club, as per The Mirror.

When asked whether he was concerned about such an outcome, Burnham - formerly the Mayor of Greater Manchester - told the BBC on Wednesday: "I would be really concerned to lose them.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester. Obviously, the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is."

Everton supporter Burnham faced significant backlash for his remarks, prompting Downing Street to respond with a statement on Thursday. A No.10 spokesperson said: "The Prime Minister made clear the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules.

"He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected. If wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."

Burnham further noted in his interview that he anticipates his interactions with City during his tenure as Mayor will withstand any potential scrutiny. "Oh indeed," the PM affirmed.

"I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn't just put into the Etihad and the campus around it but also into the city, but yes of course."

title: Man City not 'above the rules', says No 10 after backlash to Burnham remarks
description: The prime minister said he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners sell up after Premier League rule breaches.
fullText:
Downing Street has said Manchester City are not "above the rules" after Andy Burnham was criticised for his comments about the club's breaches of Premier League financial rules.

The prime minister said on Wednesday he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners decide to sell up after City were found guilty by an independent commission of most of the 115 charges they faced.

His remarks were branded "completely out of touch" and "extraordinary" by the Tories and took many in the football community by surprise.

In a statement following the backlash, Downing Street said the PM had made clear "the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules".

In an attempt to clarify the PM's position, a No 10 spokesperson added: "He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.

"Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."

Man City deny any wrongdoing and have until Friday to submit an appeal.

Sources told BBC Sport that City are expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

The Premier League said City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

In an interview on Wednesday with the BBC's political editor Chris Mason, Burnham - who was mayor of Greater Manchester until June - said he was "not getting directly involved in the process", saying it must be undertaken independently by the Premier League.

He said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and it would be "wrong" to "jump to a conclusion".

Asked if he was worried the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, a royal and the United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister - might sell up, Burnham said: "I would be really concerned to lose them.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

"I can't intervene 

In response, the Tories accused Burnham of "publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues" and questioned whether "political pressure" was being applied.

Shadow minister for sport Louie French called for the government to "keep politics out of football and ensure the Premier League's independent commission can do its job free of outside influence".

"The club face unprecedented allegations and fans are horrified by what they are reading in the papers," the Tory MP said.

"Yet Burnham is publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues. Fans will rightly ask whether political pressure is being applied here and how it relates to the owners' well-reported investments in Manchester.

"Football must be governed independently, with the rules applying equally to everyone. Fans deserve confidence that no club or owner is above those rules."

And Lib Dem MP Anna Sabine, the party's spokesperson on sport, said: "Fans of every club deserve to know the rules apply to everyone... Burnham needs to remember he's prime minister for everyone, not just Manchester."

It comes as the chairwoman of the Commons Treasury committee, Labour MP Dame Meg Hillier, wrote to HMRC on Thursday to ask for reassurance that it has "seized of the importance" of the case for any potential tax implications.

In his BBC interview, Burnham also said he was "of course" confident that his own interactions with City's owners as Greater Manchester mayor would stand up to scrutiny.

He compared City's situation to how the club he supports, Everton, had been charged with a more minor breach of Premier League financial rules in 2023, but said he "hold[s] the view very firmly that they weren't fairly treated in that process".

Burnham made his comments amid widespread shock in football about the scale of the independent commission's findings – and the strength of Premier League comments about City's actions.

The independent panel that found City guilty of rule breaches will hold a sanctions hearing – which could take months to convene – to decide the punishment, which could include a huge fine or points deduction.

City have maintained their innocence of all the accusations made.

The chairman of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) – set up by the government in 2025 – said the case had raised "serious issues".

In a statement, David Kogan said the IFR "has powers to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives and we will use these powers where appropriate", while "taking account of the findings made by the Leagues".

He added that proceedings remain ongoing and he hoped for a quick resolution.

title: Haaland 'no different' following Man City verdict
description: Norway colleagues say the striker has been unaffected by the headlines around the Premier League club ahead of the Nations League game with Wales
fullText:
Erling Haaland has been unaffected by the "sham contract" verdict against Manchester City, according to the Norway camp he's been with since the news broke.

Haaland will play for the first time since the Premier League's confirmation of City's financial rule breaches when Norway take on Wales in Cardiff on Thursday (19:45 BST).

The 26-year-old was kept away from the media before and after Norway's Nations League defeat by Portugal on Sunday after reports of City's guilty verdict first emerged.

As expected, Haaland was not put in front of the cameras as the World Cup quarter-finalists arrived in Wales amid headlines over his club and what next for the former champions, who continue to deny any wrongdoing.

Haaland signed for City in 2022, four years after the last of the nine seasons they were found to have broken financial rules, and is seen as their biggest star.

He trained as normal at Cardiff City Stadium on Wednesday evening, with Brentford defender Kristoffer Ajer saying Haaland had been "no different" since the news broke.

Manager Stale Solbakken attempted to deflect questions, tersely saying Haaland was "very good" and "scoring goals" before admitting he did miss one chance against Portugal he would normally have finished.

But asked if he had to speak to the forward because of the extra focus, Solbakken replied: "What we speak about is between him and me."

Ajer did offer more of an insight, saying Haaland remained fully focused halfway through this four-game Nations League window.

"He's been exactly the way he's always the same with the national team," said Ajer.

"He's truly focused on the upcoming games. I think he's trying to do the same as everyone else, wait and see what the outcome is - but right now the main focus is Wales tomorrow night. That's clearly been his way of doing it."

Asked if he had seen a difference in Haaland since the news broke, 59-cap Ajer said: "No not at all. Ever since I met him brings lot of energy and joy to the group.

"The biggest compliment I always give is that he hasn't changed a bit from the moment I met him even though he's the biggest star on the planet right now.

"He's been exactly the same the last few days as well which is not a surprise for me."

Haaland - who scored in the 2-1 defeat by Portugal in Oslo and twice in the 3-2 win over Denmark to make it 65 in 57 appearances for his national side - could link up with Arsenal midfielder Martin Odegaard.

Ajer added he could see similarities between the sides, saying: "It's a similar population and the same work ethic from both countries.

title: Punish Man City this season, say other club chiefs
description: Manchester City's punishment for breaching Premier League rules should be handed down before the end of this season, senior football figures tell BBC Sport.
fullText:
Manchester City's punishment for breaching Premier League rules should be handed down before the end of this season, senior football figures have told BBC Sport.

The Premier League said on Tuesday that City had been found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of its financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

They included artificially inflating revenue by more than £900m through "sham" sponsorship deals.

City have repeatedly denied guilt and signalled an intent to lodge an appeal by the end of this week.

There have been fears that the process, which has taken three years since City were charged, could be drawn out for much longer.

However, senior figures within football have told BBC Sport they see no reason why the case cannot be concluded by the end of this season.

Speaking on condition of anonymity, one club official said: "It benefits everyone for this to be resolved as quickly as possible."

When asked if they believed it would be, they said: "Instinctively yes, but it has to be done right.

"We can all see what the risks are if it's not. But those risks have been there throughout the process, as they've won the league multiple times during it."

Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? The key Man City questions

Guardiola backing Man City after guilty verdicts

Burnham 'really concerned' if Man City owners sell up after rule breaches

Another source said the process "should" be resolved by the end of the season, and they hoped any appeal would be "compressed".

The final decision rests in the hands of the independent commission, with the Premier League board - and City - able to suggest a suitable punishment before the panel makes its decision.

There is increasingly a desire to have the case resolved by the end of the season amid fears that allowing City to get to the end of the campaign without punishment could lead to uncertainty and farce, particularly if they were to win the title.

One section of the Premier League regulations says an appeal should conclude no more than 12 weeks after it is filed, and a decision should be made within 30 days of its end.

Procedures can be hurried to meet certain deadlines, like the end of a league season.

However, Ferran Soriano, the club's chief executive, has suggested the case will run for a long time.

Manchester City cannot make a further appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), but could potentially claim the process was not impartial at the High Court.

The Premier League's statement, formally announcing the guilty verdicts read on Monday, said it wants the process to be "concluded as soon as possible".

Meanwhile, City club sponsor Etihad Airways said it is considering legal action against the Premier League.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, the United Arab Emirates-based airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".

It added: "The Premier League's public communication of the commission's findings, following a period of selective leaks and reporting, has further created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings."

Etihad, City's main sponsor since 2009, also said it was given no opportunity to engage in a process that now reflects "adversely on the airline".

The statement added: "Etihad is deeply concerned by the way this matter has been communicated publicly.

"The lack of clarity and transparency, together with the selective disclosure of information, has created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the published decision.

"The Premier League must take responsibility for the consequences of the way in which these findings have been presented.

title: Infantino should have no place in future of football - Pinto
description: The computer hacker who released documents which led to the Premier League investigation into Manchester City says Gianni Infantino "should have no place in the future of the game".
fullText:
The computer hacker who released documents which led to the Premier League investigation into Manchester City says Fifa president Gianni Infantino "should have no place in the future of the game".

City have been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules over a nine-year period, though they continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.

The Premier League investigation was launched following information released into the public domain by the Football Leaks website in 2018, via German publication Der Spiegel, and following a separate investigation by European football's governing body Uefa.

In a message on X, external, Rui Pinto, creator of Football Leaks, repeated allegations from 2018 that Infantino intervened to help City and Paris St-Germain avoid financial fair play sanctions from European football's governing body Uefa.

According to a report by Der Spiegel, external, the clubs overvalued sponsorship deals to help meet FFP rules and, when facing sanctions over the matter, the allegations in the documents state Infantino helped arrange more lenient punishments for them in 2014.

A PSG statement at the time said it "has always acted in full compliance with the laws and regulations enacted by sports institutions" and it "denies the allegations".

"Since the introduction of Financial Fair Play, Paris St-Germain have been one of the most audited and scrutinised clubs in history," the club added.

"Back in 2014, there was a man who was already aware of the irregularities involving Manchester City," 37-year-old Portuguese Pinto wrote on Wednesday.

"The infamous Gianni Infantino, then Uefa general secretary, abused his authority, shared confidential documents and, in short, outmanoeuvred the investigatory chamber, doing everything in his power to ensure that both Manchester City and PSG would merely receive a fine, avoiding a deeper investigation that could have led to a Champions League ban.

"All of these details were also revealed through Football Leaks.

"Given his actions as Uefa general secretary and, more recently, as Fifa president, I can only say, in my humble opinion, that Gianni Infantino has become a cancer on football and should have no place in the future of the game."

When the allegations first surfaced, Uefa stressed that it was within the remit of the general secretary to assist in such matters, adding: "This may include discussions, meetings, assistance to help find solutions, and other interactions to assist the [investigating body] in its work."

Infantino similarly pointed to how his "job entails having discussions, having conversations, exchanging documents, drafts, ideas, whatever, on many, many, many, many, topics.

"So if then this is being portrayed as something bad, I think there's not much I can do more than my job in an honest way, in a professional way and trying to defend the interests of football."

BBC Sport has contacted Fifa following Pinto's latest statement.

Infantino has come under increasing pressure following his now-shelved plans to sell stakes in the World Cup.

European football's governing body Uefa accused Infantino of "criminal mismanagement" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, while the Swiss Football Association (SFV) is the latest association to withdraw its support for the Fifa president.

"The decision follows a comprehensive reassessment of developments over the past few months," an SFV statement read.

"From the SFV's perspective, various incidents raise fundamental questions regarding leadership, governance, transparency and decision-making processes within Fifa."

Both Fifa and Uefa are based in Switzerland.

Infantino will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate.

title: 'Business as usual' for Man City Women despite Premier League guilty verdicts
description: Manchester City manager Andree Jeglertz said it was "business as usual" for the women's team despite the Premier League charges against the club.
fullText:
Manchester City manager Andree Jeglertz did not comment on whether he had received assurances that the women's team would not be impacted after the club was found guilty of Premier League financial breaches.

Jeglertz, who joined City last summer, said it was "business as usual" and when asked about how the women's team could be affected, added: "I don't want to comment more around that."

There were seven questions in total posed to Jeglertz relating to the charges before Manchester City's press officer requested the media moved away from it.

The club has been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

The Premier League said City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.

The women's team were the first representatives of the club to address the media since the guilty charges were confirmed by the Premier League.

It is still unknown what impact the charges could have on the women's team, though BBC Sport understands there is no active investigation taking place from WSL Football.

The charges, which were breaches of Premier League rules, are different financial regulations to the WSL and they came at a time when the women's league was under the governing body of the Football Association.

There is no suggestion so far that any WSL opponents have expressed concern for City's charges, or whether they believe it has helped the women's team progress.

City defender Jade Rose said the women's players had received "the same messaging the public has" from the club.

When asked about the charges raising any concerns for the players, she added: "I'm just here to talk about the football. That's what we're focusing on."

The team took part in an open training session earlier on Wednesday morning and there did not appear to be any changes to their routine or behaviour.

Therese Sjogran, director of women's football at Manchester City, was in attendance for training, as she often is.

There were a few additional media in attendence for Jeglertz and Rose's press conference to preview their Women's Champions League game against Real Madrid.

Jeglertz responded to former men's manager Pep Guardiola's statement on social media, which voiced his support for the club.

Asked whether Jeglertz also stood beside the club, he said: "Definitely. I am working at the club now so that's who I am hired by and working with, so, for sure."

Jeglertz also said he did not find it more challenging to prepare for Thursday's game despite the noise surrounding the club.

"I don't think so. We have been training like normal and doing the work we can do to affect the game," he said.

"We haven't changed anything, we have just kept on doing everything we normally do. Definitely the thing the club has been presented, is the information we have inside of our group.

"We can't talk about anything else and we don't need to talk about anything else at the moment."

Jeglertz added that he was not frustrated by the negative media attention despite City's strong start to their WSL campaign.

The defending champions currently have 12 points from their opening four matches in the WSL and are top of the table.

They face Real Madrid on Thursday (20:00 BST) in their second Women's Champions League league phase match, having drawn their opener against Bayern Munich last week.

title: The Premier League footballers studying to become sporting directors
description: Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, Taiwo Awoniyi and others have been juggling education with a football career - even studying on the team bus during away trips.
fullText:
The scene resembles an Oxbridge graduation ceremony, but those gathered in caps and gowns are in fact Premier League footballers or former players who have won major honours in Europe and around the world.

The 2026 cohort of graduates from the PFA Business School includes Everton midfielder Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, Coventry City striker Taiwo Awoniyi and a host of well-known figures.

In the event at Arsenal's Emirates Stadium, Cesar Azpilicueta tells the group how studying on the morning of the 2021 Champions League final helped take his mind off the occasion before he captained Chelsea to a 1-0 win over Manchester City in Porto.

Dewsbury-Hall, 28, travelled by train from Merseyside to London to attend the ceremony and, despite being in the best form of his career, explains why he had completed a postgraduate diploma in global football sport directorship.

The former Leicester City and Chelsea player tells BBC Sport: "I hope I've got a long time left in football. But as a person, I'm always trying to learn and develop away from the pitch. I don't want to stop playing and then just sit around doing nothing.

"This was something that genuinely interested me. Whether I use it in the future, we'll see, but it's always good to do it now rather than wait until you've finished playing.

"If the time ever comes when an opportunity presents itself, luckily I've got something that can help me."

The assembled players are potential leaders in football's future.

Awoniyi, 29, joined Coventry from Nottingham Forest during the summer, and he remains part of Nigeria's squad as they attempt to qualify for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations.

The striker has also continued his studies throughout his playing career.

"I've got a degree in business management and another diploma, so this is my third qualification," he says.

Awoniyi's father, Solomon, has previously spoken about his strict approach to education. At times it almost prevented his son from pursuing a career in football, but Awoniyi progressed from the Imperial Soccer Academy to Liverpool before making his name in German football with Union Berlin.

"I say to people I am a quiet dreamer," says Awoniyi, who was born in Ilorin, Nigeria. "I always felt education was important. It was a promise I made to my dad that if I played football, I would keep studying.

"That's what I have done and I am proud of it."

Awoniyi points to the "ups and downs" he has experienced as a footballer, referencing the serious injury he suffered in May 2025 when he was placed in a medically induced coma after rupturing an intestine in a collision with a goalpost when playing for Nottingham Forest against Leicester City.

To him, it is important to keep improving and to recognise there is more to life than football, which is where the Professional Footballers' Association course comes in.

Awoniyi says: "It's not like a 9-5 job in football. We go in and sometimes finish quite early and, although it's challenging, I think every footballer has time in the evening for something like this business school.

"Of course, it demands a lot from you and it's all about how willing you are to do it. I say to people there are a lot of things that are bigger than football.

"Yes, football is our passion, but we are normal human beings as well and maybe that's something the world doesn't always see."

The graduates certainly appear no different from anyone else celebrating an academic achievement, exhibiting their pride.

Awoniyi has brought members of his extended family to the ceremony, while Dewsbury-Hall seeks out former Everton midfielder Tim Cahill, now working in Qatari football, to discuss the art of scoring goals.

"Obviously there are stereotypes around footballers," Dewsbury-Hall says.

"But in every industry there are smart people and there are people who aren't so smart. You'd be surprised how many intelligent people there are in football.

"Maybe some players just don't want to do things like this, but they easily could. It's just not their passion.

"I'm not saying this is my passion, but it's something I've done to show that footballers can complete these kinds of courses while they're still playing. Who knows where it will lead?"

The course is designed to run alongside a football career. Seminars are scheduled to minimise clashes with matches and training sessions.

Players can study in their own time, although Dewsbury-Hall says he has had some "weird looks" while studying on an iPad during journeys home from away games.

Every graduate has a different story.

For Wycombe Wanderers defender Steve Cook, who captained Bournemouth in the Premier League earlier in his career, the course marked a return to formal education for the first time since his school days. Having already obtained coaching badges, he knows he is approaching the end of his playing career.

Some may not actively use their newly gained expertise for many years. All will benefit in some way, though, believes Azpilicueta.

"It's not only about preparing for life after football. It's about becoming a better version of yourself in your football career as well," the former Spain defender, who retired from playing at the end of last season, tells BBC Sport.

Education has been part of his life and is what helped him become a leader on and off the pitch.

Azpilicueta built a career after turning professional with hometown club Osasuna at the age of 17.

He had continued studying until that point and, after abandoning his degree when he became a professional footballer, he later returned to complete an MBA at Harvard University in the United States during his nine-year spell at Chelsea.

The desire to study before playing the biggest match of his club career, Chelsea's Champions League final triumph five years ago, indicates how he balanced his two interests.

"Normally I'd have a nap after lunch if the game was later in the day, but that day it was impossible. You could hear the fans and you knew a big game was coming up. Having my studies also helped me focus and improve myself away from football," he explains.

After ending his playing days with Atletico Madrid and Sevilla, Azpilicueta says he will not be rushing into his next role.

The PFA course includes sessions from prominent figures, such as Brighton chief executive Paul Barber, designed to help students understand how different areas of the football industry operate.

For now, many remain focused on playing football. But among this year's graduates might be future coaches, executives and sporting directors who go on to influence the game in different ways.

title: Richards 'devastated' by Man City guilty verdicts
description: Former Manchester City defender Micah Richards felt "absolutely devastated" after reading the Premier League's "damning" verdict on the club's financial charges.
fullText:
Former Manchester City defender Micah Richards says he felt "absolutely devastated" after reading the Premier League's "damning" guilty verdict on the club's financial charges.

An independent commission found that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

The league confirmed City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, and all but one in relation to failure to co-operate with the investigation.

The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.

During that nine-year period the Sky Blues won the Premier League three times, with Richards part of their title-winning squad in 2011-12.

"The reports were troubling," he said on The Rest is Football podcast. "I saw the words which were used by the Premier League in 'sham contracts' and I felt absolutely devastated.

"I was at that club since I was 14 years old, I would die for that club. I achieved my dream at Manchester City, but then to hear these reports, and not only me as an ex-player, but the fans, what they have to go through, absolutely devastating."

While Richards was part of the City's youth academy he lived in 'digs' with a local family who are long-term supporters of the club.

The 38-year-old added: "My digs man, he rang me and he was literally in tears and asking me about information, which I don't know. I haven't got the answers to tell him.

"That's someone who's supported the club for 60-odd years and the uncertainty around it is just heartbreaking.

"To have a headline of this nature for a club that I love so much, it's been difficult. If you listen to the reports, they are damning.

"I feel saddened, I feel angry, I feel a little bit confused because, on the other side, you have City's side of the story."

City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said in a statement on Saturday that the club is still confident of proving its innocence, while on Tuesday chief executive Ferran Soriano said in a video message, external to staff and players that "irrefutable evidence" had been "ignored" by the commission.

City won their second Premier League title in 2013-14, overtaking Liverpool during the run-in to finish two points above the Reds.

"The players were told everything was fine. What the [City] hierarchy are coming out with now, they're just gaslighting.

"I think the titles should be taken off their list. Whether other clubs get them is probably slightly different. City have not just hurt their own players."

The 2013-14 season was the closest that Carragher's long-time team-mate Steven Gerrard came to winning the Premier League title.

"Those players will never get that feeling and it was robbed by Man City," Carragher added on Sky Sports News.

"No-one remembers the medal. Giving trophies or medals back, it doesn't mean anything. It's not about medals, it's about feelings."

title: The intricate web Man City spun to con the Premier League
description: The 40-page document which confirmed Manchester City were found guilty of inflating sponsorship income makes fascinating reading. Here's what it sets out.
fullText:
"To cheat, trick, deceive, delude with false pretences; to impose upon, take in, hoax."

That is the Oxford English definition of the word "sham".

And that word appears eight times in the independent commission's ruling published on Tuesday, which found Manchester City guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of financial rules, and all but one in relation to a failure to co-operate with the investigation.

The 40-page document makes fascinating reading.

It catalogues how the club's owners, Abu Dhabi United Group, knew from the 2009-10 season that there would be major overspends if the club was to reach the level they wanted to get to.

So, the ruling says, City found a way to boost sponsorship income. Season, after season, after season.

The report shows how the club's owners were topping up the value of the deals.

The so-called Disguised Funding Scheme is the central plank in a series of charges that Manchester City have been found guilty of by the Premier League.

This scheme managed to hide more than £830m of sponsorship funding, while other devices hid £90m in expenses.

We break down the key findings from the document.

Manchester City were bought by Abu Dhabi investors in 2008 but, the document says, their predicament had become clear from the start of the 2009-10 season.

These were ambitious new owners who did not just want the club to be competitive. They wanted to have the best players and be winners.

That was not going to be possible without spending more money. And lots of it.

Total losses for the 2009-10 campaign were going to exceed what was, at that time, the record single-season financial loss by a Premier League member club. That was Chelsea FC in 2006, of £140m.

According to the ruling, that was a record that the City owners were adamant the club should not break

The club knew they would likely continue to suffer large losses for at least the following five seasons.

This was when both Uefa and the Premier League were about to bring in financial fair play rules.

This was clearly going to be a problem.

To address this the only option was to significantly increase commercial revenue - and reduce the reliance on their owners.

In early 2010, Manchester City took the first steps to get the additional funding into the club.

City would enter into sponsorship agreements which were record amounts and were significantly above fair market value.

It is referred to as the 'disguised funding scheme'.

This is how it worked, according to the ruling.

The sponsorship deals were split into two parts: a base fee, and a tagged sum.

The sponsors would pay the base fee.

And the club's owners would pay the tagged sum.

Ergo, the sponsors would not have to pay the full value of the contract. The club's owners would pay the vast majority, which enabled them to invest in players.

This, the document states, "gave the misleading impression to third parties (including regulators and its auditors) in its financial statements and any required FFP returns that its commercial revenues from sponsorship agreements were far, far greater than was in fact the case".

But the club also knew they had to be nimble.

From time to time the disguised funding scheme would be tweaked to "assist with continued concealment" and "reduce the likelihood of difficult questions being asked".

What did this all mean in reality?

Commercial income from sponsors totalled £949.94m in the seasons from 2009-10 to 2017-18.

The ruling says only £119.25 million represented base fees.

A total of £830.69 million represented tagged sums - the amount paid by the club's owners.

Man City have denied the claims and say the Premier League had misunderstood the sponsorship agreements.

However, the panel said it "rejected that explanation as untrue".

It said it was "concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the disguised funding scheme".

An example given of the disguised funding scheme in action: plugging an unexpected shortfall in May 2013.

Less than a week before the end of that 2012-13 financial year the club knew they were £9.9m short of complying with Uefa's financial rules.

In a matter of days, without sponsors even being approached, a number of modified sponsor agreements were generated which increased recorded sponsorship fees to pay bonuses for events that had already taken place and to pay for a US tour.

The feared Uefa FFP shortfall was thus "plugged".

The story of Man City and 115 charges

In 2012, City launched what it called Project Longbow.

The ruling does say many of the strands of Project Longbow were genuine, and legitimate attempts to achieve the aims of boostings revenues and reducing operating losses.

One strand was not genuine, according to the ruling: the Fordham Arrangement.

This was an agreement between City and a third party called Fordham which was, according to the ruling, "little more than a front".

Funds from the club's owners "would be used (and were used) to enable Fordham to acquire from the club (at a sizeable, artificially-inflated price) the club's entitlement to benefit financially from its players' image rights".

It was a "further device by which funds could be paid into the club in a manner that concealed their true origin".

And this "enabled the club to pretend that such funds represented operating income".

In the financial statements wrongly recorded as operating income was the sum of £24.5m, and £49.414m was wrongly excluded from operating expenses.

The ruling says said the Fordham Arrangement was "operated with the knowledge and approval" of a number of individuals whose names were redacted.

Another way the club attempted to pass the financial rules was to move expensive contracts for players and managers off the books.

This was done by paying remuneration, or wages, through third parties. In reality this was being paid by the owners.

This was "instead recorded in a consultancy agreement" and "concealed the true extent of the club's liabilities".

There are three separate cases attributed to this, with all names redacted from the document. These may be published when the full written reasons are released.

City used this method for payments of £8.866m, £7.4m and £0.5m.

Manchester City vs The Premier League

"By its conduct the club clearly intended to circumvent the Premier League rules.

"The club made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League investigation".

This is another damning section, which brings into question the integrity of undisclosed people associated with City.

City served witness statements or documentary evidence from 24 individuals, most of whom who gave evidence at the hearing.

This could be problematic at a later date, as the new Independent Football Regulator is able to look at the honesty of integrity of directors and owners.

At present, no one has been named so we do not know the position of the people the ruling referred to.

It said that the evidence given by a number of important factual witnesses "was false in a number of key respects".

It added that certain factual witnesses provided evidence "that they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest".

The ruling also said that City knew that the annual accounts "did not provide a true and fair view of the financial position" and that the club "was reckless as to whether those annual accounts provided a true and fair view".

All in this, it was said, showed that City failed to act "with utmost good faith" and "breached duties of co-operation that it owed to the Premier League".

This is how the club's financial statements for the seasons between 2009-10 and 2017-18 did not show a true and fair view of the financial position:

Income from overstated by over £830m

Wrongly excluded expenses by £8.866m

Wrongly excluded expenses by £7.4m

Wrongly excluded expenses by £0.5m

Wrongly recorded as operating income £24.5m

Wrongly excluded expenses totalling £49.414m

title: Man City found guilty of Premier League charges and ‘overstating income by £830m’
description: Man City strongly maintain their innocence and claim to have ‘a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence’ to defend themselves, but an independent commission has found them guilty of ‘sham contracts’ and misleading accounts
fullText:
Manchester City have been found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules over a nine-season period.

An independent commission, which was appointed following a four-year investigation to rule over the charges which stretch between 2009 and 2018, ruled that the current Premier League leaders had "sham contracts" arranged for a number of its commercial partners.

The findings also detail how City "relied on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs," while the club reacted to the verdict by underlining they were "disappointed and surprised by the opinion."

And while sanctions are yet to be decided, the verdict, which was widely reported last Friday, has now been confirmed.

A Premier League statement read: "An independent Commission has found Manchester City FC guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules over a 9-season period, and the majority of charges in relation to its failure to co-operate with the League's investigation.

"The independent Commission found that Manchester City arranged 'sham' commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were only required to pay a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees."

The verdict is counter to the strong statements from chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and CEO Ferran Soriano, who adamantly voiced their confidence in City's innocence.

City stated that "the Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

"The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence."

And despite stating Manchester City had until Friday, 2 October to appeal, the club confirmed in a statement that they will "pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe."

The Premier League released a 40-page document with details surrounding the case, concerning the hearing dates from 16 September to 31 October 2024, titled: "The Football Association, Premier League Limited and Manchester City Football Club Limited."

City have been accused of not acting in "utmost good faith" while also failing to "provide a true and fair view of the Club's financial position," with the commission finding that their income over eight seasons was "hugely overstated by over £830m".

While the independent commission also found that "the club made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League investigation" and "breached duties of co-operation."

Part of the findings concerned Man City's fear that they would exceed a record single season financial loss, held by Chelsea in 2006 at £140m, and that the club was "adamant it should not break."

The Premier League began its investigation into Man City in December 2018, with a complaint subsequently issued under Section W of the League's rules in February 2023.

And despite the independent Commission holding a 42-day hearing, which concluded in December 2024, it has taken 21 months for the verdict to arrive.

The independent Commission insisted it was "regrettable" it had taken so long to arrive at a decision, with 7,000 pages of evidence.

"This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history. There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches. title: Why Salisbury are 'bigger than many Premier League teams' in Kuwait
description: Sixth-tier Salisbury FC have a unique relationship with Kuwait, where they are regarded as "bigger than many Premier League" clubs.
fullText:
As with every home game, the Salisbury FC players and coaching staff went to embrace the fans in the Andrews Terrace at The Ray Mac Stadium after Saturday's 2-0 win against Folkestone Invicta.

Alongside the normal applause and cheers, they were greeted with a chant that isn't a regular from the songbook.

"Kuwait away ole, ole," sang fans of the National League South outfit.

The players clapped back with an extra buzz - within 24 hours they would be travelling to the Middle East.

"Straight away we all said, 'yeah, we're all in," explains Salisbury player Luke Russe.

"It's a unique opportunity and as players, we are so thankful to everybody involved in making this trip happen. I've been involved in this level for a long time now and I've never had an experience like it."

The five-day trip involves the club facing one of Kuwait's most successful teams on Wednesday, Al Qadsia, who have won more than 50 trophies, before returning on Thursday to play Saturday's FA Cup third qualifying round against Dulwich Hamlet.

It comes as part of the club's continued link with Kuwait through their owner Ali Alhamad, who purchased the club in 2025.

The club hopes the trip will offer significant commercial growth and, for the players, an opportunity to experience football in a new environment and culture.

The Mohammad Al-Hamad Stadium holds 22,000 spectators, more than five times that of Salisbury's The Ray Mac.

"We'd love to win the game," says Russe. "But at the same time I think it's more about the experience and about the club as a whole, going over there, living that way of life and experiencing the game.

"We've got a very young group, so for them to experience that and kind of experience cultures and differences is great.

"It'll be a fantastic opportunity for us players, for the staff, and I think it'll bring the whole club even closer to what we are now."

The players will get to visit local restaurants, try local food and coffee, visit schools and universities, and hold a question and answer session for locals to understand how an English football club operates from the perspective of owner Alhamad.

"It will help the players themselves with opening up their horizons into different cultures, different countries, experiencing other footballing nations and other styles of football," he says.

The country's interest in Salisbury is evident.

Four of the club's sponsors are from Kuwait, including the front of shirt sponsor for a company that created the country's first Sharia-compliant digital bank, and the training kit represents a popular Acai company that can only be bought in Kuwait.

On Instagram the official Arabic account of Salisbury FC has more than 14,000 followers - only slightly fewer than their official English profile.

When the squad arrived in Kuwait they were greeted by a small group of fans, while school children interacted with them as if they were Premier League players.

"I would even go further than saying that Salisbury in Kuwait is bigger than many of the Premier League teams in the UK," says Alhamad.

"So I am not exaggerating when I do say that it is a huge name in Kuwait but what's more important than the size is we are contributing a lot to the local community here in Kuwait and to the children and the future of the football in Kuwait.

"Salisbury really is an integral part of opening those avenues and helping the youth here to be better in all the aspects we're looking for."

The eagerness the players showed shocked Alhamad, with all of the squad, except Jaiden Bartolo who is on international duty, agreeing to go within an hour.

Along with the cultural experience, the club is also using this as a way to grow financially, with all ticket sales and advertisement money going to Salisbury.

Meanwhile, Salisbury have set up a summer camp in the country and ran a trial session where the top three players trained with the first team during pre-season.

"It's quite simple in my mind. If you do what other people do, you'll just get the same results everyone else does," says Alhamad.

"Football in England, especially in the non-league, is a brutal business. So just throwing in money to the football club with the aim of getting promotion is fool's gold, in my opinion.

"The right way to do it is to build it properly all the way from the bottom and if you just limit yourself to one market, which is the city or town that you are in, that is pretty limited.

"With social media and the avenues we have, such as being in Kuwait and the Gulf and Arab regions. That's a huge untapped market that is thirsty for English football."

People in Kuwait are avid watchers of the Premier League but non-league is still very much an unknown commodity in the country.

"People are not properly educated in the fact that the non-league is actually a really high quality and that is also an indirect goal of mine with this match," he adds.

"We're here to show them, you're belittling, playing the sixth tier of English football, the second step of the English non-league.

"We'll show you what we have and you never know, maybe the sixth tier of English football will beat the top tier on the biggest team in Kuwait.

This growth in Kuwait will offer Salisbury FC an important opportunity that is rare for a National League South team.

But ensuring The Whites remain strongly embedded within the local community in the city will also be vital, with the FA Cup on Saturday the first test on their return.

"I have grown to love it and love the people of Salisbury and the towns around it," says Alhamad.

"It's a great place to be. And that's what I'm really focusing on not just in a trip here in Kuwait, also in our heart and soul, our fans, our community, which is Salisbury."

title: What Sheffield United Need to Do to Get Back to the Premier League
description: Sheffield United have not started their 2026/27 Championship campaign particularly well. Results have been mixed, and the Blades currently sit in the middle of the table, a position that feels uncomfo...
fullText:
Sheffield United have not started their 2026/27 Championship campaign particularly well. Results have been mixed, and the Blades currently sit in the middle of the table, a position that feels uncomfortably familiar for a club that has yo-yoed between the top two divisions for most of the past decade.

If you check the most reputable football betting markets, the odds tell a clear story: Sheffield United are not among the favourites for promotion. Bookmakers see a team with real quality in certain areas, but also one with structural problems that remain unresolved.

Those odds are not unfair. But they are not the final word either. Sheffield United need to get a few things right this season, and if Chris Wilder and his staff address them, the picture could change significantly before May.

STOKE ON TRENT, ENGLAND – SEPTEMBER 19: Lamine Cissé of Stoke City and Jamal Baptiste of Sheffield United during the Sky Bet Championship 2026/27 match between Stoke City and Sheffield United at Bet365 Stadium on September 19, 2026 in Stoke on Trent, England. (Photo by Barrington Coombs/Getty Images)

Sheffield United have consistently been a possession-oriented side under Wilder. They move the ball forward with intent; they create chances, and against the weaker half of the Championship table, that approach has produced very good results. The issue is what happens when it stops working, and against better-organised sides, it stops working more often than it should.

The pattern last season was fairly consistent. United's attacking play leaned heavily on a small group of players to produce moments of quality. When those players were in form and available, the team looked genuinely dangerous.

When they weren't, the side struggled to find an alternative route. The team had no reliable aerial threat, little variety in crossing delivery, and little to make a defensively solid opponent uncertain about their approach. Teams knew what was coming, and good teams dealt with it comfortably.

Fixing this does not require a complete tactical overhaul. It requires adding some variety: a bigger striker who offers a presence in the box, or the tactical discipline to overload wide areas and stretch defensive shapes in a different way. The Blades have the creative quality to hurt teams through the middle. What they need is something that makes defending them from a low block just a bit more uncomfortable.

One of the genuinely impressive things about this Sheffield United side is how aggressively they press. They win the ball high up the pitch more consistently than almost any other team in the division, and when the press clicks, it creates turnovers in dangerous areas that lead directly to chances and goals.

The problem comes when the press does not work. High pressing creates space in behind by design. When you push your defensive line up and commit players forward, you gamble that the press succeeds. When it does not, you are exposed.

Sheffield United conceded far too many goals from counter-attacks last season, and that directly stemmed from the press breaking down without enough recovery structure behind it. The counter-press (the second moment of pressure after the initial press fails) was too disorganised too often.

The solution here is mostly about discipline and organisation rather than personnel. The best pressing teams in Europe accept that the press will occasionally be beaten, and they have a clear plan for what happens next. United need that clarity at defensive transition. The pressing itself is a strength worth keeping. The vulnerability it creates is a problem worth solving.

SHEFFIELD, ENGLAND – SEPTEMBER 13: Andre of Wolverhampton Wanderers is tackled by Oliver Arblaster of Sheffield United during the Sky Bet Championship 2026/27 match between Sheffield United and Wolverhampton Wanderers at Bramall Lane on September 13, 2026 in Sheffield, England. (Photo by Gareth Copley/Getty Images)

Sheffield United created plenty of chances last season. That is not in dispute. The issue is that across the squad, the conversion rate was consistently below what the numbers suggested.

Too many players underperformed their expected goals over the full season, and that is not bad luck; at that scale, it points to a finishing problem that needs direct attention.

Set pieces deserve particular attention here. United consistently generated high-quality chances from dead-ball situations, but the goals they scored from those opportunities did not reflect the quality of the positions they found themselves in. A large part of that comes down to squad composition, specifically, a lack of height and aerial ability.

When you consider how many headed goals top Championship sides score from set pieces each season, United's tally stands out as a real weakness. Bringing in players who can compete physically in both boxes would have a disproportionate impact on results relative to the cost.

Every analysis of Sheffield United this season eventually comes back to the same point: the team's ceiling is very high when its best players are available and performing, but the drop-off when they are not is too steep.

Over a Championship season, relying on a handful of individuals is a significant risk. Injuries, suspensions, and loss of form are inevitable; what matters is whether the squad can absorb them.

Wilder has spoken about injecting fresh ideas into the group this season, and the coaching staff has seen some changes. Whether those changes translate into greater tactical flexibility and squad cohesion remains to be seen.

But the message from the top is that the team is not standing still. The challenge now is turning that intention into results. A stronger, deeper squad with more physical variety and better options from the bench would give United a far better chance of sustaining a promotion push through the second half of the season, when the games matter most, and the margins get tightest.

title: Pochettino: Manchester City verdicts show fans ‘lived through an era of deception’
description: US men’s national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino expressed dismay at news of Manchester City being found guilty of widespread financial improprieties on Monday, saying that fans “lived through a period of deception” because of City’s alleged financial impropriety.  The Guardian and other outlets have reported that Manchester City have been found guilty by the Premier League of violating the vast majority of 115 different charges concerning violations of financial rules between 2009 and 2018.  Pochettino was the manager of Tottenham Hotspur for five seasons, from 2014 to 2019, and of Southampton before that from 2013 to 2014.
fullText:
US men's national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino expressed dismay at news of Manchester City being found guilty of widespread financial improprieties on Monday, saying that fans "lived through a period of deception" because of City's rule breaches.

The Guardian and other outlets have reported that Manchester City have been found guilty by the Premier League of violating the vast majority of 115 different charges concerning violations of financial rules between 2009 and 2018.

Pochettino was the manager of Tottenham Hotspur for five seasons, from 2014 to 2019, and of Southampton before that from 2013 to 2014. He also took charge of Chelsea for a single season in 2023-24.

"Where were the controls?" Pochettino said in Spanish, when asked by the Guardian for his thoughts on the guilty verdicts. "That's what gets my attention. Where were the controls?

"If I remember being at Southampton, then Tottenham – I remember building [the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium] and not having the economic possibility of a transfer for 18 months. I think we were the only team in the history of the Premier League with 18 months without [making a transfer].

"If a team like us, Tottenham, was fighting for titles with those above us and every year in the top four, getting to the semi-finals of Champions League without being able to do a transfer for 18 months, all because we needed to get used to the [Premier League financial controls]? They were so strict with us but also so lenient with others. Because of that, that's why I say: it's all very strange."

Manchester City's issues started when a 2018 investigation by German paper Der Spiegel showed potential financial improprieties, citing leaked internal documents, outlining a host of potential violations occurring over a 10-year span between 2008 and 2018.

City – who have always denied the allegations – were subsequently charged by the Premier League in 2023 of falsifying details of their finances, with some of those issues centering around payments to players and coaches. They have also been accused of violating Uefa's financial fair play regulations, and the Premier League's own profit and sustainability rules (PSRs).

Uefa made an attempt at disciplining City in 2020, banning the club from Uefa-sanctioned competition like the Champions League and fining them €30m. That punishment was later overturned by the court for arbitration of sport; some of the violations, they said, occurred too long ago to be punished and others weren't adequately proven.

City are widely expected to appeal against the Premier League's verdicts in the next two weeks and the ensuing legal proceedings could drag out for an extended period.

When asked what he feels a potential punishment should be, Pochettino again expressed his disappointment at the overall situation.

"Whatever punishment [they choose], it's impossible to turn back time," he said. "It's done a lot of damage, more than anything the guidelines. At the end of the day many clubs followed the rules and some didn't. Maybe they thought that the punishment [wouldn't come for a lot of years] – what are they going to do? An economic punishment? Docking points? It's really hard.

"It's sad," Pochettino continued. "It is a huge sadness. At the end of the day we get into a situation where what got celebrated wasn't that real, what seemed good maybe wasn't so good, what didn't look good maybe was good but couldn't be good because of what happened. At the end of the day, we went through something where sporting fairness didn't exist. So, how do you repair everything that was damaged because of that, if it's true all of the 114 rules that were broken, we've lived through a period of deception."

Last week, Pochettino offered his thoughts on the punishment handed down to Chelsea, who were found guilty of similar violations on a much smaller scale. Chelsea were Premier League champions in 2016-17, with Pochettino's Spurs finishing in second place. The club was later fined heavily by the Premier League for undisclosed payments to players, coaches and other involved parties. The club was also hit with a nine-month academy transfer ban.

"We should win one title, one Premier League," Pochettino told UK-based media last week. "They were punished, they admitted, so that's it? The title should be for the team that was second … It's true that we didn't compete with the same rules. OK, now we can say that they scored goals, they won games, and like this. OK, that's it, but it's completely fair to say that we didn't compete before the start of the season with the same card."

"Maybe with the same rules, if we apply the same things, maybe we could've signed some players that would have made the team better or scored more goals," said Pochettino. "It's not me complaining. It's the truth. If they admitted they broke the rules, the Premier League title was for the second best team."
